messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Drug Use: take drugs, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Niran was thirty-one, a married carpenter who had built a steady life in the United States after growing up in a South Eastern Asian family that prized keeping calm, working hard, and not making trouble. The night that unsettled that life began as an ordinary evening drive home, with the usual fatigue of the job in his shoulders and the loose plan to get dinner with his wife once he finished a quick errand. He was stopped by police and, in the confusion that followed, he was hurt by officers in a way that left him shocked, humiliated, and frightened. What stayed with him most was not only the physical force itself but the feeling that the situation had moved beyond anything he could control or explain. In the hours and days after, he kept replaying every step in his mind, trying to sort out what he should have said differently, whether his voice, his timing, or his posture had somehow made things worse. He repeatedly blamed himself for what happened, returning again and again to the same impossible question of how he could have avoided it.

In the months that followed, Niran found himself thinking about the event even when he was trying not to. He would catch himself revisiting the scene while driving, while eating dinner, or while lying awake after his wife had fallen asleep. These thoughts were not organized or comforting; they came as fragments and arguments with himself, and he often ended up in the same cycle of self-reproach. He tried to push the whole thing out of mind, telling himself that he should not dwell on it and that it would only make him feel worse, but the more he tried to keep away from it, the more the memory seemed to hover at the edge of his day. At work as a carpenter, that effort became especially difficult. He noticed that standing in a half-built room with no clear exit or turning his back to a doorway made him uneasy, so he began arranging himself with his back against a wall whenever he could, scanning the space instead of settling into the job. On job sites, where delays are routine and deliveries, measurements, or other workers’ timing often change the pace of the day, he found himself assuming something bad was happening whenever a task took longer than expected. A stalled truck, an unanswered call, or a supervisor taking too long to return could send him immediately toward the worst conclusion, his mind racing to some unspecified danger before he had any facts.

This sense of being unable to let go spread into his evenings as well. Even in places he knew were safe, such as his own home, he found that he could not relax in the way he once had. Sitting on the couch with his wife, he remained tense, listening for sounds outside, watching who entered a room, and choosing seats that let him keep an eye on the whole space. He had come to feel that being comfortable meant letting his guard down, and letting his guard down felt dangerous. His wife noticed that he seemed distant and keyed up, though he did not always have the words to explain it; he would say only that he could not switch off, that his body did not seem to understand that the day was over. Because he did not want to keep turning the incident over in his head, he sometimes used drugs to blunt the thoughts and take the edge off the agitation that settled in after work or late at night. For a while this gave him brief relief, but it also became one more thing he had to manage in secret, adding strain to his marriage as he tried to keep the extent of his distress from showing.

Over time, Niran’s world narrowed in small but noticeable ways. At work he became more watchful and less able to settle into long stretches of routine labor, and at home he chose positions in rooms as if mapping out escape routes and sight lines. He no longer trusted delays to be ordinary, and he was rarely fully at ease anywhere, even when nothing was happening. What brought him to seek help was the growing exhaustion of living in this state and the strain it was placing on his relationship with his wife, who could see that he was carrying something heavy and was worried by how much he was using drugs just to get through the day. Niran came hoping for some way to stop blaming himself and to feel safe enough to sit in a room, do his work, and sleep without waiting for something terrible to begin again.
